title: Is a Heat Pump Cheaper Than Gas, and Does It Pay for Itself?

scenes.purpose: Open on two neighbours with opposite results from the same decision.

visual.description: Split field: "Smaller bill" lands on the left in green on "smaller heating bill"; "Bigger bill" lands on the right in red on "bigger one".

scenes.direction: Cold open; the second line punches in on "bigger one".
scenes.narration: Picture neighbours on the same street who put in heat pumps the same autumn: by February, one has a smaller heating bill and the other a bigger one.

scenes.purpose: Pose the two questions the video answers.

visual.description: The question types on, large and centred; "cheaper" and "pay for itself" take the two colours from the previous scene.
onScreenText: Cheaper than gas, and does it pay for itself?

scenes.direction: Hold on the question through s03.
scenes.narration: Neither of them is lying. So is a heat pump actually cheaper to run than a gas furnace, and does it ever pay for itself?

scenes.purpose: Give the savings pitch in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "$300 to $500" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "should be able to save you $300 to $500 in energy cost each year"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in; hold half a second after the quote.
scenes.narration: The channel Atlas AC makes one case: heat pumps "are more energy efficient than gas systems and should be able to save you $300 to $500 in energy cost each year".

scenes.purpose: Give the opposite view in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "not true" turns red as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "for most people, that is not true"

scenes.direction: Wipe from the previous quote card.
scenes.narration: Jonathan Tracey, comparing his own heat pump's costs with gas, says the opposite: "when you're told that having a heat pump will save you money, the reality is for most people, that is not true".

scenes.purpose: Name the catch: electricity costs more than gas per unit of energy.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "four times the price of gas" holds and turns amber.
onScreenText: "electric's four times the price of gas"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: Guy Martin, testing a heat pump on his channel, put the catch in one line: "Trouble is, electric's four times the price of gas, so it's all meeting the middle."

scenes.purpose: Turn the disagreement into a question the arithmetic can answer.

visual.description: The question types on centred; "efficiency" in green, "price" in red.

scenes.direction: Hold through s08.
scenes.narration: So which wins: the efficiency, or the price? The arithmetic fits in one line.

scenes.purpose: Lay out the break-even rule step by step.

visual.description: A three-line sum builds one line at a time: the price ratio, then the furnace efficiency, then the seasonal COP to beat, which holds in amber.

scenes.direction: Each line lands as its words are spoken.
scenes.narration: Divide the price of electricity by the price of gas, for the same amount of energy, and multiply by the furnace's efficiency: a heat pump whose average efficiency over the season, its seasonal COP, beats that number heats the home for less.

scenes.purpose: Put the 2024 US numbers into the rule.

visual.description: Two tiles: the price ratio on the left, the break-even seasonal COP on the right, each landing as it is spoken.

chart.title: 2024 US average prices

points.label: Seasonal COP to match a high-efficiency furnace

chart.note: National averages; the bar differs by state.

citations.label: EIA, 2024 residential electricity and gas prices

scenes.direction: The tiles land on "3.45" and "3.28".
scenes.narration: At 2024 US average prices, electricity cost 3.45 times as much as gas for the same energy, so a heat pump needed a seasonal COP of 3.28 to match a high-efficiency furnace.

scenes.purpose: Show that the bar moves from state to state.

visual.description: Three horizontal bars, the number of states in each break-even band; the low band grows first on "11 states", the 3.0-or-higher band last and longest.

chart.title: States by the seasonal COP that beats a 95% gas furnace
chart.note: Counts include the District of Columbia; annual average prices.

scenes.direction: Bars build in band order as the sentence names them.
scenes.narration: State by state, that bar moves: in 11 states, Florida and Texas among them, a seasonal COP of 2.5 beats that same furnace, while in most of the rest it takes 3.0 or more, in places from California to New York.

scenes.purpose: Show the rule's caveat in the source's own words.

visual.description: The EIA method note scrolls in; the line about fixed monthly customer charges highlights as "fixed monthly charge" is spoken.

excerpt.highlight: they include fixed monthly customer charges

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps on "fixed monthly charge".
scenes.narration: Those are averages, and the rule leaves things out: it ignores time-of-use rates and backup resistance heat, and an average gas price includes the fixed monthly charge, which a home that keeps its gas hookup still pays and one that disconnects saves.

scenes.purpose: Turn from the place to the machine.

visual.description: The question types on centred.
onScreenText: Does the heat pump you buy clear it?

scenes.direction: Hard cut; hold half a second.
scenes.narration: So where you live sets the bar. Does the heat pump you buy clear it?

scenes.purpose: Show how much the heat pump's performance changes who saves.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars for gas homes with air conditioning: the lowest performance level short, the highest nearly full; each grows as its figure is spoken.

chart.title: Gas homes with AC that would save on bills

scenes.direction: Bars grow on "38 percent" and "99 percent".
scenes.narration: Researchers at the national laboratories NREL and Lawrence Berkeley estimated bills, at the energy prices of winter 2021 to 2022, for American homes that heat with gas and already have air conditioning, and the share that would save ranged from 38 percent to 99 percent, depending on the heat pump's performance level.

scenes.purpose: Add the gas homes without air conditioning, and show the shares depend on prices.

visual.description: The two bars stay; two shorter bars for gas homes without AC grow beneath them on "lower still". On s16 the whole chart dims slightly.

chart.title: Gas homes that would save on bills
chart.note: Modelled bills; at older prices the shares are lower.

scenes.direction: New bars build on "lower still"; the dim lands on "2019 prices".
scenes.narration: For gas homes without air conditioning, the shares were lower still, partly because those homes start paying to cool with the heat pump. And those shares move with energy prices: at 2019 prices, the researchers found, fewer gas homes would save.

scenes.purpose: Move from models to measured homes.

visual.description: The question types on centred.

scenes.direction: Hard cut.
scenes.narration: What happens in real homes?

scenes.purpose: Show the British result in the paper's words: less energy, slightly higher cost.

visual.description: The working paper passage; "40% decrease" marks first, then "slightly higher running costs" highlights as it is spoken.

citations.label: Bernard et al. 2024, NBER working paper (UK homes)

scenes.direction: Highlight lands on "slightly higher".
scenes.narration: In Britain, a study of homes that replaced a gas boiler with a heat pump found their total energy use fell by 40 percent, yet because electricity costs more per kilowatt-hour than gas, the running costs came out slightly higher.

scenes.purpose: Put the British running-cost gap and the gas connection in figures.

visual.description: Two tiles in pounds: the extra yearly running cost in red, the yearly gas connection charge saved by disconnecting in green.

chart.title: Heat pump vs gas boiler, Octopus standard prices, June 2024
chart.note: British prices in pounds; not a forecast for a US furnace.

citations.label: Bernard et al. 2024, NBER, at Octopus Energy prices

scenes.direction: Tiles land on "£190" and "£100".
scenes.narration: At Octopus Energy's standard prices in June 2024, that came to £190 a year more than the gas boiler, though a home that cuts off its gas connection saves about £100 a year of that: a British result at British prices, not a forecast for an American furnace.

scenes.purpose: Show that a time-of-day tariff changed the result.

visual.description: The Cosy passage; "Switching to Cosy saves customers" highlights as "saved money" is spoken.

citations.label: Bernard et al. 2024, NBER, Cosy tariff

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps on "saved money".
scenes.narration: The same working paper then looked at Cosy, Octopus's own tariff that prices electricity by the time of day, and estimated that customers who switched to it saved money against Octopus's standard tariff, most of it from shifting their use into cheaper hours.

scenes.purpose: Show that a tariff only helps a heat pump controlled to use it.

visual.description: The RMI Houston passage; "saves around $1,000 in net present cost" highlights on "around $1,000".

excerpt.highlight: saves around $1,000 in net present cost

scenes.direction: Highlight lands on "$1,000"; hold a beat.
scenes.narration: In the US, an RMI model of Houston found a tariff is not enough by itself: a standard heat pump on a free-nights plan cost more than on a flat rate, and only one controlled to heat and cool ahead while power was free saved, around $1,000 in net present cost.

scenes.purpose: Answer the running-cost question.

visual.description: Two lines build one per clause: the first in green, the second in red.
onScreenText: AC already, well-performing heat pump: usually cheaper

scenes.direction: Each line lands with its clause.
scenes.narration: So is a heat pump cheaper to run than gas? For a gas home that already has air conditioning and gets a well-performing heat pump, the national model says it usually is; with a weaker unit, it often is not, and the more your electricity costs next to your gas, the better the heat pump has to be.

scenes.purpose: Retire the halved-bill claim against gas.

visual.description: A single line sets large; "still paid more" turns red.

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: And if you have heard that a heat pump halves the bill, against gas the evidence here does not back it: the British homes cut their energy use sharply and still paid more.

scenes.purpose: Turn from running cost to payback.

visual.description: Split field: "Running cost" on the left greys out, "Payback" on the right lights up.

scenes.direction: Wipe left to right on "the other half".
scenes.narration: But running cost is only half of the decision; the other half is whether those savings ever pay back the price of the heat pump.

scenes.purpose: Give the payback pitch in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "by year five" turns amber.
onScreenText: "could be offset in savings by year five"

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: The pitch is that they do, and fast: Atlas AC tells viewers that "the increased cost to convert a gas system to a heat pump could be offset in savings by year five".

scenes.purpose: Put the viewer's own furnace into the question.

visual.description: The question types on centred after a short hold on the empty field during s28.
onScreenText: Is that pitch true for you?

scenes.direction: Type on with s29.
scenes.narration: Now picture your own gas furnace: it is not new, but it still works. Is that pitch true for you?

scenes.purpose: Set out how the studies compare costs.

visual.description: One line sets large; "extra" holds in amber.

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: The national laboratory model, and a second study by Deetjen and colleagues, set the comparison up carefully: they count only what a heat pump costs beyond replacing the old heater with a similar one, at the end of its life.

scenes.purpose: Show how often a heat pump comes out ahead before subsidies, by efficiency level.

visual.description: Three horizontal bars: the minimum-efficiency heat pump first and longest, then the two more efficient models shorter, each growing as its figure is spoken.

chart.title: Homes ahead before subsidies, over the heat pump's life
chart.note: All US homes, every heating fuel; not gas homes alone.

scenes.direction: Bars build on "55", "41" and "21 percent"; hold through s32.
scenes.narration: Even on that footing, the national laboratory model found the best single option, a cheaper minimum-efficiency heat pump, came out ahead before subsidies in 55 percent of homes, and the more efficient models cost more up front, which cut the share to 41 and 21 percent. That group takes in most homes heated with oil, propane or electricity, and, of the gas homes, most of those with central air in a warmer climate.

scenes.purpose: Give the second study's national figure and its verdict on gas.

visual.description: One large tile: the share of US single-family houses that would gain, landing on "21 percent".

chart.title: US single-family houses that would gain from a heat pump
chart.note: All heating fuels; switching from gas rarely pays.

citations.label: Deetjen et al. 2021, by heating fuel

scenes.direction: Tile lands on "21 percent".
scenes.narration: Deetjen's study found that only 21 percent of American single-family houses would gain economically from replacing their heater with a heat pump, and that switching from natural gas rarely pays even when the old heater is due, with almost no houses in cold climates where it makes sense.

scenes.purpose: Set the British net cost against the tariff savings.

visual.description: Two tiles in pounds: the 20-year net private cost lands on s34, then the Cosy savings value lands beside it on s35, slightly larger.

chart.title: UK gas boiler to heat pump, 20 years

points.label: Cosy tariff savings, if they persist

chart.note: British pounds; the tariff savings assume they persist for 20 years.

scenes.direction: First tile on "£4,121", second on "£4,675".
scenes.narration: In Britain, the same study as before put the net private cost of swapping a gas boiler for a heat pump at £4,121 over 20 years, what the household pays after a grant, and that already subtracts the boiler the household no longer has to buy. But the authors valued the Cosy tariff's savings, if they persisted, at £4,675, more than that net cost.

scenes.purpose: Turn to timing.

visual.description: Wipe to a plain field with "When you buy" centred.

scenes.direction: Wipe on the sentence; hold half a second.
scenes.narration: Which brings us to when you buy.

scenes.purpose: Show how the extra cost collapses when the old equipment has to be replaced anyway.

visual.description: Three tiles, extra cost of the heat pump: nothing broken first, then the air conditioner failed, then furnace and air conditioner both, the last in green.

chart.title: Extra cost of a cold-climate heat pump, Minnesota
chart.note: Propane homes with a propane furnace as backup, not gas homes.

scenes.direction: First tile on "$9,450"; the air conditioner tile on "air conditioner alone"; the last on "$370".
scenes.narration: A Minnesota study priced a cold-climate heat pump with a propane furnace as backup at $9,450 installed: with nothing broken, that whole price was the extra cost, and the payback ran to well over a decade, depending on the furnace it was compared with. When the air conditioner alone had failed, the payback roughly halved, and when the furnace and the air conditioner both needed replacing, the extra cost fell to $370 and the payback to about a year or less.

scenes.purpose: Keep the propane result from being read as a gas result.

visual.description: One line sets large; "not gas" in red.

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: Those homes ran on propane, not gas, so the years themselves do not carry over to a gas home.

scenes.purpose: Show the same exception for gas homes from two other studies.

visual.description: A list builds one line per sentence: the RMI exception, then the Lawrence Berkeley finding.
onScreenText: Replacing a furnace and an air conditioner
Adding cooling as well as heating

scenes.direction: Each line lands as its sentence names it.
scenes.narration: For gas homes, RMI's model finds the same exception: in many retrofits a heat pump costs more than new gas equipment, except for the customer who must replace both a furnace and an air conditioner, because a single heat pump does both jobs. And in Lawrence Berkeley's cost study, the heat pump's price premium over gas equipment disappeared once a home was getting cooling as well as heating.

scenes.purpose: Answer the payback question.

visual.description: Three lines build one per clause: working furnace in red, both due or adding cooling in green, only the air conditioner due in amber.
onScreenText: Furnace and AC both due: little or nothing extra
Only the AC due: shrinks, does not vanish

scenes.direction: Each line lands with its clause; hold after the last.
scenes.narration: So does a heat pump pay for itself? For a gas home whose furnace still works, the evidence says it rarely does on energy savings alone; bought when the furnace and the air conditioner both need replacing, or when the home is adding cooling anyway, the extra cost can shrink to little or nothing, while with only the air conditioner due it shrinks but does not vanish.

scenes.purpose: Remind the viewer the averages are not their house.

visual.description: One line sets large and holds.
onScreenText: None of these is your house's number

scenes.direction: Hard cut in.
scenes.narration: And even within one area, the national laboratory study found bill savings varied more from house to house than from place to place, so none of these figures is your house's number.

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer with what to do before signing.

visual.description: A checklist builds one line per instruction.
onScreenText: Do the sum with your own prices
Get the quote now; decide when both are due

scenes.direction: Lines land with their clauses; hold 2 s on the full list.
scenes.narration: So before you sign, do the sum from earlier with your own prices and your furnace's efficiency, and ask the installer for the seasonal COP of the unit they are quoting. And if your furnace still works, get the quote now, and decide when the furnace and the air conditioner are both due.
